article.title: Trump threatens to raise tariffs if Mexico does not stop a new migrant caravan
article.author: Pablo Meriguet
article.content: A new caravan of Latin American migrants heading north through Central America has brought to the fore the Trump administration’s anti-immigration policies and its pressure campaign on Mexico to stop the thousands of participants before they reach its borders. The administration of Republican Donald Trump reported that it is following the news closely with concern. In this regard, the US president threatened Mexico with doubling tariffs if it does not stop the caravan: “Here we go again! With the perceived loss by the Republicans in the midterms … the INVASION of our country is taking place again … They will not be accepted! MEXICO MUST STOP THEM, NOW, and if they do not do so, the tariffs on Mexico will be IMMEDIATELY DOUBLED,” Trump said in response to the possibility of the arrival of nearly 1,500 people, although that number could rise. Since the start of his second term, Trump has threatened to raise tariffs on Mexico if it did not impose greater complications and obstacles on Latin American migrants seeking to reach the United States across its borders. Since then, both countries have reached a series of agreements to more actively prevent migrants from crossing. Whether this is a genuine concern, a way to pressure Mexico, or a new tactic to win more votes, Trump’s statements regarding the arrival of migrants at the southern border have not gone unnoticed. Through economic threats, diplomatic pressure, and demands for military and intelligence cooperation, Trump has demanded that Mexican authorities detain migrants even before they reach the US border. In February 2025, Trump signed an additional 25% tariff increase on Mexican products, asserting that the Sheinbaum administration was not doing enough to prevent the arrival of migrants. In response, the Mexican government agreed to deploy 10,000 National Guard members to its northern border in exchange for the US increasing its controls on weapons entering Mexico from US territory, as well as the suspension of the extraordinary tariff measures. Mexico’s response In response to Trump’s threats regarding the migrant caravan heading toward the United States, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum sought to calm tensions and stated that “no migrant caravan has reached the [US] border.” However, the Mexican president clarified that there are indeed two migrant caravans: one in the south of the country, in Chiapas, and another that has recently begun to form in Honduras. Trump decided to use the migrant caravans to explain an alleged correlation between the arrival of migrants and the Democrats’ victory in the recent midterm elections: “The invasion of our country is happening again,” without providing any evidence to support that claim … “Huge caravans are forming and beginning their illegal march through Mexico.” In her statements to the press, Sheinbaum did not rule out a connection between the two events, but she warned that this is actually a scam used by human traffickers to convince people that they can now enter the United States, thereby charging them large sums of money. “It must be said that sometimes there are people who deceive migrants and tell them, for example, that the US election results have changed immigration policy, which is false,” Sheinbaum said. When asked about the possibility of pressure from migrants, Sheinbaum said that border authorities have significant experience dealing with these issues: “The vast majority [of migrants] return to their countries of origin once they realize that, well, they can’t – they won’t be able to – cross the Mexican-US border.” A caravan of dreams and hardships The group began its journey on November 15, crossing through Honduras and aiming to reach Guatemala. Among the migrants who left their homes for various reasons are men, women, and children seeking to reach US territory to start a new life. It is currently unknown what will happen to the caravan that has dubbed itself “God with Us.” El País reported that at least 300 people were dispersed by Mexican authorities, but that the bulk of the group continues to move forward at a slow pace. “We believe we can cross. The borders may be closed, but God can open the way for us,” said José Pérez , one of the migrants seeking work in the US. He added: “Our destination is New York; we’re going to try to cross the entire border – we don’t know where, but we’re going to get there.”
